d.title: Two families, and each one is blind to exactly what the other handles
d.caption: *“Jon Smith, 12 High St”* against *“John Smyth, 12 High Street”* — **there is no exact match to look up, so you need a score between 0 and 1 and a threshold above which you call it a match. Everything in this module is either a way to compute that score or a way to choose that threshold.** And the two families are complementary rather than competing: **edit distance handles typos and is blind to reordered words; set and vector methods handle reordering and are blind to typos inside a word.**

state: each is blind to the other's strength

d.title: Three operations and a recurrence that is the best of three neighbours
d.caption: **The minimum number of single-character edits — insert, delete or substitute — to turn one string into another.** The recurrence is the whole algorithm: **each cell is the best of the cell above plus one (delete), the cell left plus one (insert), and the diagonal plus the substitution cost.** The boundary conditions carry the base case: **`d[i][0] = i` and `d[0][j] = j`, because turning a string into an empty one costs one delete per character.** And **`cost = 0` when the characters match**, which is what lets a diagonal run through for free.

d.title: One cell checked by hand, and the diagonal wins at 1
d.caption: For row `k`, column `s`: **above gives 2, left gives 2, and the diagonal gives `d[0][0] + cost = 0 + 1 = 1` because `k ≠ s`** — so the minimum is 1, which is what the matrix says. **Every cell is the best of three neighbours, and the bottom-right cell is the answer for the whole pair: 3.** The three edits it found: **`kitten → sitten`, `sitten → sittin`, `sittin → sitting`** — two substitutions and an insert.

d.title: Three cases including the empty string, all matching the reference
d.caption: The implementation reproduces all three: **`kitten`/`sitting` = 3, `flaw`/`lawn` = 2, and `''`/`'abc'` = 3.** The last is the one worth having in a test suite — **it exercises the boundary row the recurrence depends on**, and a version that initialises `d[0][j]` to zero instead of `j` passes the first two cases and fails only this one. **Which is the general shape of an edit-distance bug: the interior logic is easy and the base case is where it goes wrong.**

d.title: A transposition costs 2 under Levenshtein and 1 under Damerau
d.caption: **Levenshtein has three operations; Damerau adds a fourth — transposition of two adjacent characters, at a cost of 1.** The three cases it fixes are all the same keyboard event: **`ca`/`ac`, `teh`/`the` — the classic typo — and `Smith`/`Smtih`.** All three drop from 2 to 1. And the last row is the control: **`kitten`/`sitting` is 3 either way, because there is no transposition in it** — so Damerau is strictly a refinement rather than a different metric.

d.title: The reordered pair scores 0.0909, which is worse than two unrelated names
d.caption: **Dividing by the longer length bounds the result in [0, 1] and makes scores comparable across lengths — a distance of 2 means something very different on a 4-character string than on a 40-character one.** Then the failure the whole module exists for: **`'John Smith'`/`'Jon Smyth'` scores 0.8000 with two typos, and `'John Smith'`/`'Smith, John'` scores 0.0909 for being the same name reordered.** Edit distance is not slightly wrong about reordering — **it rates a reordering as almost maximally different.**

d.title: Three terms, and the window is what makes it not an edit distance
d.caption: **`m` counts characters appearing in both strings *within a window* of `max(|s1|,|s2|)/2 − 1` positions, each matched only once** — which is the structural difference from 8.1: **Jaro never computes a sequence of edits, it counts coincidences inside a tolerance.** The three terms are then readable: **what fraction of the first string matched, what fraction of the second matched, and what fraction of the matches were in the right order.** Range: **0 means no shared characters, 1 means identical.**

d.title: Both literature examples reproduce, and one pair gets no bonus at all
d.caption: **`MARTHA`/`MARHTA` at 0.9444 and `DIXON`/`DICKSONX` at 0.7667 are the two examples used throughout the literature, and both reproduce exactly.** The row to stop on is `JELLYFISH`/`SMELLYFISH`: **0.8963 before the bonus and 0.8963 after — no Winkler bonus at all, because the first characters differ.** **The bonus is strictly a prefix bonus**, so a leading character difference forfeits it entirely however similar the rest is. And `abcd`/`dcba` at **0.5000** is §05's liability in one number.

d.title: The lowest-scoring pair gains the most, by design
d.caption: **`DIXON`/`DICKSONX` gains 0.0466 — the largest bonus of the three — because it started lowest.** That is the `(1 − Jaro)` term: **the bonus scales with how much room is left, so a pair already at 0.95 can gain at most 0.05 × 0.4, while a pair at 0.7 can gain much more.** Which means the Winkler bonus **helps borderline pairs across a threshold and barely moves pairs that were already clearly matching** — a deliberate design, not a side effect.

d.title: One `break` is the difference between a correct implementation and an inflated one
d.caption: **Each character in `s2` can only be consumed once — so the `break` after a match is essential, or repeated letters would match many times and inflate the score.** The rest of the implementation is two passes: **find matches inside the window with a flag array per string, then walk the matched positions in order and count how many are out of place, halving the result.** And the Winkler wrapper is six lines: **count the common prefix capped at 4, then `j + prefix · p · (1 − j)` with `p = 0.1`.**

d.title: A perfect 1.0000 on the reordering and a flat 0.0000 on the typos
d.caption: **Order disappears at the tokenisation step — a set has no order, so the metric cannot be sensitive to it** — which is why `'John Smith'`/`'Smith John'` is **1.0000** and the three-word reorderings are too. Then the exact mirror of 8.1's failure: **`'John Smith'`/`'Jon Smyth'` scores 0.0000, because not one token is shared.** And the comma row shows the brittleness of word tokens: **`'Smith, John'` scores only 0.3333, because `'Smith,'` is a different token from `'Smith'`.**

d.title: The two metrics are each near-zero on exactly the pair the other handles
d.caption: This is the clearest table in the module. **Edit similarity scores the typo pair 0.8000 and the reordered pair 0.0909. Word Jaccard scores the typo pair 0.0000 and the reordered pair 0.3333.** Neither is a weak version of the other — **they fail on disjoint inputs**, which is why §03's character n-grams exist and why 8.5's `token_sort_ratio` exists: **both are attempts to be good at both columns at once.**

d.title: Every pair gets a non-zero score, and no pair gets a perfect one
d.caption: **A single typo destroys only the few n-grams that span it**, so the typo pair rises from 0.0000 to **0.1538** — and the reorderings fall from 1.0000 to between 0.4167 and 0.7273, because reordering breaks the n-grams at the joins. **That is the trade: n-grams are the only representation here that scores every one of these pairs sensibly, and the price is that nothing scores 1.0.** Choosing `n` is real: **2 is tolerant and collides, 4 or 5 is discriminating and brittle, 3 is the usual default for names.**

d.title: Five differences, and the one that decides it is weighting
d.caption: **Jaccard treats tokens as present or absent; cosine works on counts or weights, so a token appearing three times contributes more than one appearing once — and the vectors can carry TF-IDF weights rather than raw presence.** Which is the row that matters for 8.4: **all tokens equal against any weighting**, because real record data is full of tokens that are present and uninformative. The length row is the other practical difference: **Jaccard penalises different sizes through the union; cosine normalises it away.**

d.title: Limited scores 1.1335 and Beta scores 2.3863
d.caption: **Jaccard and plain cosine treat every token as equally informative, and in real record data that is badly wrong: *Limited*, *Corporation*, *Street*, *Road* appear everywhere and tell you almost nothing, while *Acme* or an unusual surname is nearly decisive.** The idf column is that intuition as a number over a seven-name corpus: **`limited` at 1.1335 because it is in almost every name, and `beta`, `gamma`, `holdings` all at 2.3863 because each appears once.** Note **`ltd` also scores 2.3863** — which is §03's abbreviation problem showing up in the weights.

d.title: Acme Corp Ltd ranks fifth, below three companies that are not Acme
d.caption: The ranking is the failure. **`Beta Corporation Limited` scores 0.6615 and `Acme Corp Ltd` scores 0.4017 — so the metric prefers a different company with matching boilerplate over the same company abbreviated.** TF-IDF down-weighted `limited` to 1.1335, **and three shared tokens at low weight still beat one shared token at high weight.** Which is why §03's answer is normalisation rather than a better metric: **no weighting scheme fixes a string that shares almost nothing with its own abbreviation.**

d.title: Four normalisation steps, and the first one alone fixes §02
d.caption: **Stripping legal suffixes turns §02's comparison into *Acme* against *Beta*, which ranks correctly** — one step, and the failure is gone. Standardising abbreviations is the other half: **`Corp → Corporation`, `St → Street`, or `Acme Corp Ltd` and `Acme Corporation Limited` share far fewer n-grams than they should.** Then two structural points: **compare the name and the legal form as separate fields with separate thresholds**, and **fit idf on your actual corpus — a generic one will not know that *Limited* is ubiquitous in yours.**

items.sub: Ltd, Inc, LLC, plc, GmbH, Corporation, Co

d.title: Five properties, and two of them are about operating it rather than scoring
d.caption: The first two are accuracy: **down-weighting common tokens stops legal suffixes dominating, and running it over character n-grams combines idf weighting with 8.3's typo tolerance.** The last three are why it stays the default after twenty years of alternatives: **sparse vectors make candidate retrieval sublinear through an inverted index, you can print the idf of any token and explain a score, and there is nothing to train — fit on the corpus you are matching, no labels needed.**

d.title: One pair, five scorers, 48.5 to 100.0
d.caption: **These are libraries, not algorithms — they wrap edit distance in ready-made scorers returning 0 to 100** — and the spread on one pair is the whole lesson: *“New York Mets”* against *“the Mets of New York”* scores anywhere from **48.5 to 100.0** depending on which function you call. **`token_set_ratio` gives 100.0 by comparing shared tokens against the leftovers, so the extra words cost nothing.** And **RapidFuzz is the modern replacement for FuzzyWuzzy: same API, C++ internals, 10–100× faster, MIT rather than GPL.**

d.title: Sorting normalises both strings to the same thing, so the score is exactly 100
d.caption: **`token_sort_ratio` sorts the words alphabetically before comparing, so `"New York Mets"` and `"Mets New York"` both become `"mets new york"` — and the score is 100.0, not approximately.** Which solves 8.1's reordering failure completely for this pair. Note the plain `ratio` disagrees with the reference: **61.5 measured against ~54 quoted** — a tokenisation or normalisation difference in the library version, **and the kind of discrepancy worth checking before trusting a threshold copied from a blog post.**

d.title: Two rows where a scorer returns 100 on strings that are not the same thing
d.caption: **`'Smith'` against `'Smith Smith Smith'` scores 100 on both `partial_ratio` and `token_set_ratio`** — the first because `'Smith'` is a perfect substring, the second because repetition becomes invisible once you take a set. And **`'cat'` against `'category'` scores 100 on `partial_ratio`.** Which is the general warning: **each scorer fixes one failure and introduces another, so `partial_ratio` on short fields will match any string that happens to be a prefix.**

d.title: A million records is 1.6 years of pairwise comparison
d.caption: **All pairs is `n(n−1)/2`, so 1,000 records is 50 seconds and 1,000,000 is 499,999,500,000 comparisons — 13,889 hours, or 1.6 years, at 10,000 pairs a second.** Which is why blocking is not an optimisation: **without it, matching is infeasible above about ten thousand records whatever your scorer costs.** And every blocking key trades recall for reduction: **exact first letter gives ~26× and misses a typo in the first character, while phonetic keys block `Smith` and `Smyth` together and are language-specific and noisy.**

d.title: Seven situations, and the last row applies to all of them
d.caption: Read it as the index to the module. **Single-token fields with typos take Levenshtein; personal names take Jaro-Winkler; multi-token fields with varying order take `token_sort_ratio` or Jaccard; typos *and* reordering together take character n-grams** — which is 8.3's measurement, where n-grams were the only representation to score every pair sensibly. **And the last row is not a choice: block first, then any of the above**, because §04 priced the alternative at 1.6 years.

state: block first, then any of the above
